PAPER: Locally Optimal Solutions to Constraint Displacement Problems via Path-Obstacle Overlaps Antony Thomasa, Fulvio Mastrogiovannib, Marco Bagliettob aRobotics Research Center, IIIT Hyderabad, Hyderabad 500032, India. bDepartment of Informatics, Bioengineering, Robotics, and Systems Engineering, University of Genoa, Via All’Opera Pia 13, 16145 Genoa, Italy. Abstract We present a unified approach for constraint displacement problems in which a robot finds a feasible path by displacing constraints or obstacles. To this end, we propose a two stage process that returns locally optimal obstacle dis- placements to enable a feasible path for the robot. The first stage proceeds by computing a trajectory through the obstacles while minimizing an appropriate objective function. In the second stage, these obstacles are displaced to make the computed robot trajectory feasible, that is, collision-free. Several examples areprovidedthatsuccessfullydemonstrateourapproachontwodistinctclasses of constraint displacement problems. Keywords: Constraint Displacement Motion Planning, Constraint Overlaps, Minimum Constraint Displacement, Minimum Constraint Removal. 1. Implementation and Implications InthepreviousSection,wehavepresentedtheconstraintdisplacementprob- lem by dividing it into two sub-problems – the overlap stage and the displace- ment stage. The overlap stage essentially optimizes a function of robot overlap withtheobstacles. Fortheminimumconstraintdisplacementproblem,inwhich 17 the robot finds a feasible path while minimizing displacement magnitudes, the overall obstacle overlap is to be minimized. This is because an obstacle needs to be displaced only if there is an overlap with the planned robot trajectory. Therefore, minimizing the overall overlap with all the movable obstacles during planning leads to minimum displacement (magnitude) during execution. The corresponding objective function is as given in (9) with h(·) being an identity function. For an MCR problem, the unique obstacle overlaps should be mini- mizedaswelookforsolutionswiththeminimumnumberofdisplacedobstacles (or minimum obstacles to be removed). A similar reasoning could be used to formulate the objective function for manipulation under clutter. An objective functionfortheMCRproblemcanbefoundinSection6. InthecaseofNAMO additional aspects such as the work done could be incorporated. This may in- volveprioritizingoverlapsatthepolygonaledgesorcontactpoints, forexample to facilitate a better grasping of the object by the robot. Toimplementtheoverlapstage,weemploytheFORCESPRO[30,31]solver, which generates optimized nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) code. In order to perform the displacement stage optimization, we employ the nonlinear optimization function fmincon [32] with the interior point algorithm [33]. The interiorpointalgorithmisusedsincethemodelsin(13)and(17)arenon-convex. This approach proceeds iteratively by starting from the interior of the feasible set and hence solicit an initial feasible point. Initial points for thedisplacement stageareeasilyobtainedbydisplacingthepolygoninthexorydirectionsothat there is no overlap. For example, in the case of a circle-rectangle overlap, an initial set of feasible points for the rectangle vertices are obtained by displacing the x or y coordinates (direction depends on the nature of the overlap) of the rectangle by an amount ∆. A safe value for ∆ is the diameter of the circle. Furthermore, if we solicit different solutions, if they exist, they can be obtained by using ∆ = ∆ ± δ, where δ > 0. However, a global optimum cannot be theoretically guaranteed for the fmincon optimization and the approach tend to return local minima. Though fast locally optimal solutions are obtained, the solutions are greatly affected by the initial and starting points. We note here that both MCD and MCR do not exhibit the optimal substructure property [34] of dynamic programming, meaning that optimal solutions to sub-problems are not necessarily optimal (a consequence of the problems being NP-hard). Consequently, optimization over the entire time step can be computationally expensive. Therefore, the MPC approach provides a very reasonable approximation. We note here that when a human moves around through a cluttered space, he or she rearranges or push the objects around to make way. Most often, the human consciously or sub- consciously performs an optimization, for example, in terms of the number of 19 objects to push or finding the shortest path. However, as the human navigates quicklythroughtheclutteredspace,mostoftenheorsheisnotconcernedabout globally optimal solutions, but locally optimal solutions that can be computed quickly through his thought process as soon as the map of the environment is registered. Discussion Our approach operates under certain assumptions. In the overlap stage, we assumethatallobstaclesareofequalimportance,specificallythateachobstacle can be displaced by exerting the same effort. This assumption is restrictive in practice (as an example, displacing a heavy table is evidently more difficult thanmovingalightweightchair). Astraightforwardwaytorelaxthislimitation is to introduce object-specific difficulty weights into the overlap computation. 25 (a) (b) Figure 13: A robot navigating from the left to the right room in an initially blocked environment, where obstacles can be displaced. The scene contains 17 obstacles, out ofwhich6arelargerandheavier. (a)TheMCRsolutionwhenallobstaclesaretreated equally; a large object must be removed to obtain a feasible path. (b) When larger objects are assigned ten times the weight of smaller ones, the MCR solution instead removes two smaller obstacles to find a feasible path. At present, the weight term (M ) associated with the overlap function in (9) i is uniform across all obstacles. This can instead be modified to incorporate object-dependent weights reflecting the relative difficulty of displacement. An illustrative example is shown in Fig. 13. In the example, adjusting such weights according to each object displacement difficulty results in a different solution to the MCR problem. A more principled approach would involve in- corporating the actual physical work to be done by the robot to move each object into the objective function. This would require modeling the manipu- lation strategy, that is, whether to push or perform a pick-and-place action, along with identifying suitable contact points and feasible trajectories. Such considerations, however, are beyond the scope of the present work. In the displacement stage, the algorithm computes the required displace- mentsoftheoverlappingobstacles. Weassumethatthecomputeddisplacements correspond to actions that can physically carried out by the robot. Although this is a reasonable assumption, in practice certain objects may not be movable tothecomputedlocationsduetofactorssuchaslimitedreachability,insufficient payload capacity, or lack of free space to execute manipulation actions. Fur- thermore,someobjectsmaybetoobigorheavy,thereforerequiringcooperative manipulation by multiple robots. Another practical consideration is the time 26 required to move each object, which could be incorporated into the computa- tionofdisplacementstoprioritizefaster-to-moveobjectsoroptimizeoveralltask duration. Addressing these aspects constitutes a promising direction for future research. In cases in which such intricacies are unnecessary, the displacement can alternatively be handled using any state-of-the-art manipulation planning approach [35, 36]. 8. Conclusion Wepresentedanapproachforconstraintdisplacementproblemsthatenables a robot to find a feasible path when constraints or obstacles can be displaced. The approach consists of a two-stage process. It begins by finding a trajectory through the movable obstacles while minimizing an objective function that de- pends on the specific constraint displacement problem. In the second stage, we calculate locally optimal displacements of the overlapping obstacles. This uni- fiedframeworkcanbeemployedtomodelvariousconstraintdisplacementprob- lems as discussed above, using the appropriate objective functions. Section 6 demonstrated the applicability of our approach to MCD and MCR problems Currently, we do not consider interacting obstacles, that is, obstacles them- selves are not collision-free. We hope to relax this assumption in the future. In future work, we would also like to provide displacement bounds for the con- straints so that the total displacements fall within the given bound. We also envision a unified framework that combines the two stages discussed herein. References [1] K. JSON: Name: overlap_displacement_pipeline Title: Two-stage overlap-penalized trajectory optimization and locally optimal obstacle displacement for constraint-displacement motion planning Short Hypothesis: A two-stage planner that (1) computes trajectories minimizing a weighted overlap penalty and (2) computes locally optimal continuous obstacle displacements will reduce total obstacle displacement magnitude by at least 10% versus sampling-based minimum-constraint-displacement baselines on cluttered 2D navigation benchmarks while maintaining equal or higher success rate. Related Work: Existing approaches to constraint-displacement motion planning fall into two broad classes: sampling/graph-based methods that search configuration space annotated with obstacle labels to minimize number of removed constraints, and rearrangement/NAMO methods that search for manipulation sequences to clear the path. Sampling-based MCD/MCR strategies iteratively grow roadmaps or sample robot and obstacle states; they provide approximate guarantees but suffer exponential state growth when obstacles overlap in C-space and in practice provide only discrete displacement decisions or obstacle removal counts rather than continuous displacement locations. NAMO and rearrangement planners incorporate manipulation costs but typically focus on discrete move/replace actions, grasp/contact selection, or greedy heuristic removal and do not optimize continuous obstacle translations/rotations jointly with robot trajectory. Prior optimization-based MPC approaches for MCD employ discrete displacement sets or ignore rotation and produce iterative heuristics with limited displacement refinement. Across these methods limitations include: inability to return continuous locally optimal displacement vectors (translation+rotation), sensitivity to combinatorial explosion in overlapping C-space regions, reliance on discrete displacement candidates, and neglect of object-specific displacement difficulty or continuous work estimates. Abstract: We address constraint-displacement motion planning where a robot obtains a collision-free path by displacing movable obstacles. We propose a unified two-stage pipeline: an overlap stage that synthesizes a look-ahead trajectory by minimizing a weighted sum of robot state cost, control effort, and continuous robot–obstacle overlap penalties, and a displacement stage that computes locally optimal continuous obstacle translations and rotations so the planned trajectory becomes collision-free. The overlap penalty encodes problem-specific objectives (e.g., total displacement magnitude for Minimum Constraint Displacement, or a binary weight promoting Minimum Constraint Removal). The displacement stage formulates and solves constrained nonlinear optimizations per overlapping polygon pair to produce rotation-aware, length-preserving obstacle moves. The main contribution is a practical end-to-end method that returns both a low-overlap trajectory and concrete, locally optimal continuous displacements, enabling evaluation on multiple constraint-displacement variants. We expect the pipeline to reduce aggregate displacement and the number of moved obstacles compared to sampling-based baselines while producing explicit displacement solutions useful for downstream manipulation or execution. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Procedurally generated 2D polygonal benchmarks: densities low/medium/high with obstacle counts N∈{10,25,50}, movable fraction p∈{0.2,0.5,1.0}, object size distributions uniform and skewed. (2) Structured scenarios from the paper: ABCD L-shaped domain, household charging-station maps, shelf-clutter retrieval-like maps (replicated as 2D projections). (3) A set of 30 randomized seeds per scenario to capture initialization variability. Baselines: (A) sampling-based MCD planner (sampling robot+obstacle displacements, discrete displacement candidates), (B) sampling-based MCR planner (minimum-constraint-removal roadmap search), (C) greedy-removal heuristic (iteratively remove nearest overlapping obstacle until a path exists), and (D) shortest-path (no obstacle displacement). Metrics: total displacement magnitude (sum of Euclidean translations plus rotation penalty), number of moved obstacles, success rate (found collision-free executable trajectory), path length, estimated manipulation work (object-specific weight × displacement), planning time (overlap-stage + displacement-stage), and robustness (mean and standard deviation over seeds). Experimental setup: robot models include circular holonomic, L-shaped planar robot (as in paper), and differential nonholonomic vehicle; dynamics and control limits follow the provided formulations. Overlap-stage parameters: lookahead L∈{11,21}, overlap weight sweep Mv∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}. Displacement-stage: continuous optimizer with interior-point method; initialization variants: (i) axis-displacement by object diameter, (ii) random perturbation, (iii) nearest-escape vector. Comparison studies: (1) Baseline comparison reporting all metrics per scenario. (2) Ablation A: discrete vs continuous displacement stage (replace continuous optimizer with discrete candidate set). (3) Ablation B: effect of lookahead L on solution quality and compute time. (4) Ablation C: effect of object-weighting (uniform vs weight proportional to 'difficulty') on MCR outcomes. Statistical analysis: per-metric paired tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank) across seeds, significance threshold α=0.05. Failure reporting: number and causes of optimizer failures and cases where continuous displacements are infeasible given constraints. Risk Factors and Limitations: Nonconvexity and local minima: the displacement-stage nonlinear optimizer is nonconvex and may return local minima sensitive to initialization; no global optimality guarantee. Initialization sensitivity: overlap-stage MPC horizon and initial guesses affect both trajectory and resulting overlaps; short horizons can yield suboptimal or oscillatory behavior. Approximation errors: polygon bounding via multiple circles introduces conservative overlap measures and may misrepresent true contact geometry, affecting displacement magnitude estimates. Execution feasibility assumption: planner assumes computed continuous displacements are physically achievable (ignores mass, friction, reachability, collision-free manipulation paths, and required force/torque). Scalability: computation time grows with obstacle count (displacement-stage per overlapping obstacle optimization and MPC complexity), limiting real-time applicability in dense scenes. Generalization limits: demonstrated in 2D planar projections; extension to full 3D geometry, articulated or deformable obstacles, and cooperative multi-robot displacement is nontrivial. Perception and uncertainty: method assumes perfect obstacle geometry and pose estimates; sensor noise, localization error, and dynamic obstacles can degrade performance. Evaluation bias: synthetic benchmarks may not capture real-world contact/interaction constraints; estimated manipulation work is a proxy that may not reflect true execution cost.
